Experimental validation of scintillator detector response to correlated neutrons with MCNP and associated packages

Matthew J. Marcatha,∗, Madison T. Andrewsa, Douglas R. Mayoa, Tyler A. Jordana,b, Michael E. Risinga

aLos Alamos National Laboratory, United States bUniversity of California Berkeley, United States

## Abstract

Time, energy, and angle correlated neutrons are emitted in nuclear ﬁssion. New, physics-based ﬁssion event generators that capture these correlations have been incorporated into MCNP6.2 because correlations can impact nuclear non-proliferation and safeguards systems response. DRiFT is a detector response code that takes MCNP outputs and reproduces laboratory analogous detector quantities. Previous work has compared DRiFT to single detector experiment data and has discussed recent updates to DRiFT speciﬁc to correlated ﬁssion experiments. This work shows a validation of recent updates to DRiFT for organic scintillator response in correlated ﬁssion neutron experiments using a 252Cf source. Outputs from MCNP with the FREYA ﬁssion event generator were post-processed with DRiFT and compared to experiment data. Simulation and experiment results are in reasonably good agreement for multiple correlated neutron quantities.

## Keywords

## 1. Introduction

Multiple, correlated neutrons are often emitted in nuclear ﬁssion and are a useful observable to identify and to quantify special nuclear material. Accurate simulations of ﬁssion neutron emission, detection, and system response are important to interpret experiment results and to develop new detection systems in the nuclear nonproliferation and safeguards communities [1]. Fission neutrons are correlated in emission angle and energy [2, 3], but these characteristics are often omitted in radiation transport codes. The physics-based ﬁssion models CGMF [4] and Fission Reaction Event Yield Algorithm (FREYA) [5] have been developed and included in MCNP6.2, a generalpurpose, continuous-energy, generalized-geometry, time-dependent, Monte Carlo radiation-transport code [6]. Both of these models follow an excited ﬁssion fragment through de-excitation to produce neutron and gamma-ray correlated emissions. These ﬁssion models capture neutron angular and energy correlations. Users are cautioned to limit their use to correlated outputs from these ﬁssion models, because the prompt ﬁssion neutron spectra do not agree with evaluated spectra [3]. Models outside of MCNP6.2 have also been developed to simultaneously reproduce ﬁssion neutron energy and angular correlations [7]. The ability to model detector system response to correlated neutrons is particularly important for organic scintillator experiments (EJ-301 in this work). Organic scintillators are sensitive to fast neutrons primarily through scattering on hydrogen, therefore organic scintillators are prone to crosstalk – when a single neutron causes detection events in multiple detectors. These detectors are useful for neutron time-of-ﬂight and cross-correlation measurements because they have nanosecond order time resolution. Given the utility of organic scintillators in correlated neutron measurements [8, 9, 10, 11, 12], it is important to have accurate ﬁssion models and detector system models. DRiFT, a Detector Response Function Toolkit, is under development at Los Alamos National Laboratory [13, 14]. DRiFT is a toolkit which uses MCNPTools [15] to take MCNP PTRAC output, to apply detector system response models, and to output realistic detection event data. The MCNP PTRAC card allows the user to generate an output ﬁle of particle track events. A validation of uncorrelated response from DRiFT was shown [13]. Previous work has detailed DRiFT developments to address the simulation of correlated ﬁssion experiments. The work shown here is a validation of DRiFT correlated re-

This work shows DRiFT correlated response validation by making comparisons to experiment data. The experiment neutron-neutron coincidence data for validation includes event frequency with angle, event detection time difference, and event pulse integral distributions. While other neutron-neutron experiment work has been done [16, 17, 18], this work focuses on MCNP6.2 and DRiFT correlated response validation with the collected experiment data.

## 2. Methods

2.1. Experiment Figure 1 shows a cross-section, in a plane parallel to the ﬂoor, of the ﬁve 7.62-cm thick by 7.62- −cm EJ-301 detector array with the detector faces 20.4 cm from a center point modeled in MCNP. The EJ-301 (a BC-501A equivalent) organic scintillator is pulse shape discrimination (PSD)-capable and has nanosecond time resolution [19]. Each scintillator is coupled to a 9821B ET-Enterprises photomultiplier tube (PMT). Additional experiment details will be discussed in Section 2.2. In two separate measurements, the detector faces were each 20.4 cm and 50.4 cm from a central 252Cf source. Background data were taken without the 252Cf source in place. The detectors are separated by 45◦for each measurement. A 0.5-cm thick tungsten cap was ﬁt over each detector volume to attenuate gamma rays incident on each detector. Using a 252Cf source of 3.58 × 104 ﬁssions per second at the time of measurement, the 20.4-cm and 50.4-cm source-detector case observed approximately 1.89 × 1010 and 2.13 × 1010 ﬁssions, respectively. Charge integration PSD was performed on each waveform to classify the event as a neutron or photon detection [19, 20]. Figure 2 shows a heatmap of the ratio of the integral over the tail to the integral over the whole waveform plotted against the total integral. A neutron-induced waveform will have a relatively larger tail than a gamma-ray-induced waveform of the same total integral. 252Cf experiment data shown in Fig. 2 shows two distinct regions, where neutron events lie primarily above the red discrimination line and gamma-ray events are primarily below the line. The data were analyzed with a lower light output threshold of 0.1 MeVee or approximately 0.19 V · ns. The conversion from V · ns to MeVee was estimated with a calibration measurement of the 137Cs Compton edge location. A proton recoil of 0.77 MeV would produce a 0.1 MeVee event. 2.2. MCNP6 and DRiFT simulations The experiment setup and surrounding room were modeled in MCNP in great detail [21]. A unique model was created for each source-detector distance. The source was 252Cf spontaneous ﬁssion and used either the FREYA ﬁssion model option [5] or the default 252Cf spontaneous ﬁssion treatment [22]. The default treatment uses an evaluated neutron spectrum and neutrons are only time correlated in multiplicity. Only neutrons and protons were tracked in transport. Neutron and proton source and bank events were recorded to the PTRAC ﬁle. DRiFT parameters were set to emulate detector, digitizer, and source speciﬁcations. The source activity in the DRiFT’s TimeDistribution module [23] was set to 3.58 × 104 ﬁssions per second. In the Scintillation module, the detector type was set to EJ-301 with a 9821B ET-Enterprises PMT. The PMT applied high voltage was set to

1500 V. Light output response to proton recoils used data from Cecil et al. [24]. In the Digitizer module, the parameters were set to the CAEN V1730 speciﬁcations. The voltage range was 2 V and the dynamic range was 14 bit. The sampling frequency was 500 MHz with 256 samples per waveform. The short and long integral gates for PSD were set to 18 and 300 ns, respectively. For the PSD data in Fig. 2, the total integral is over the full 300 ns and the tail integral is the diﬀerence of the total and short integrals. Detection event information was written to a ROOT TTree [25]. ROOT is a data processing framework developed at European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN). Detection information includes long and short waveform integrals, and detection time for each detector channel.

## 3. Analysis and Results

Previous work has shown DRiFT’s ability to reproduce singles pulse integral histograms [13]. Here we demonstrate continued agreement of singles pulse integral histograms in Figs. 3 and 4 and then show comparisons to correlated experiment data to validate recently added features. All references in the text to correlated events or coincidences refer to neutron-neutron coincident detection.

3.1. Pulse Integral Distributions Figures 3 and 4 compare the FREYA and default MCNP ﬁssion treatment to the experiment data. Both experiment and simulation detection event data were histogrammed by pulse integral. Individual detector channel count rates varied by at most 3%. Background pulse integral distributions were subtracted from the experiment 252Cf pulse integral distributions shown in Figs. 3 and 4. Background data were analyzed using the same algorithms as in the 252Cf data analysis. Total background neutron count rates were approximately a factor of 300 lower than 252Cf neutron rates for the 0.1 MeVee threshold. Figure 3 shows the absolute count rate for both experiment and simulation. In Fig. 3, the total singles rate of the FREYA result at 20.4 cm underestimates by 19.5% and at 50.4 cm underestimates by 27.2% where the default model at 20.4 cm underestimates by 20.7% and at 50.4 cm underestimates by 28.3%. 3.2. Correlated Distributions Figures 5 through 10 show a validation of MCNP and DRiFT’s ability to reproduce correlated ﬁssion neutron quantities with comparison to experiment data. Each correlated distribution is a measure of neutron-neutron coincidence events: one correlated by detector angle (Fig. 5); one correlated by neutron detection time diﬀerence (Figs. 6-8); and one by pulse integral against detector angle (Fig. 5). The uncertainty propagation for correlated distributions assumed each detector pair is statistically independent. The correlated quantities also capture cross-talk and room return eﬀects. Crosstalk occurs when a single neutron causes multiple detection events. The DRiFT output includes a cross-talk ﬂag to mark correlated events as such. Cross-talk is most prevalent where detectors have higher solid angles relative to one another. Using simulated data where cross-talk events are easily identiﬁed, the estimated cross-talk is approximately 6%, 2%, 1%, and 0.8% of the total doubles rate for the 45, 90, 135, and 180◦pairs in the 20.4 cm. Cross-talk is approximately 6%, 2%, 0.8%, and 0.4% of the total doubles rate for the 45, 90, 135, and 180◦pairs in the 50.4 cm. Room return occurs when a neutron is detected after interacting in surrounding laboratory material.

3.2.1. Coincidences against detector angle Figure 5 shows the neutron-neutron doubles rate plotted against detector opening angle. For this experiment, there are four 45◦, three 90◦, two 135◦, and one 180◦pairs. Each angle is normalized by the number of pairs for that angle. Again, due to uncertainty in the source rate, the total simulation neutron-neutron rate is normalized to the experiment rate. The 20.4 cm simulation results were normalized by a factor of 3.64 and the 50.4 cm simulation results were normalized by a factor of 3.01. The background neutronneutron doubles rate against detector opening angle was subtracted from the 252Cf doubles data. The neutron-neutron background rate was estimated to be 0.5% of the rate with the source in place. MCNP and DRiFT reproduces the trend in neutron-neutron doubles against detector angle at both detector standoﬀdistances. After normalization, the 90◦simulation pairs underestimate by 16% and 13% for the 20.4 cm and 20.4 cm cases, respectively. The 180◦simulation pairs overestimate by 17% and 14% for the 20.4 cm and 20.4 cm cases, respectively. There are more counts toward zero and 180◦because neutrons are boosted by fully accelerated ﬁssion fragments which are emitted back-to-back in 252Cf [26]. The FREYA result over-predicts the count rate at 180◦, consistent with results

3.2.2. Coincidences against detection time diﬀerence Figures 6 through 8 show the distribution of time-diﬀerences between coincident neutron detection events. Accidental background was averaged over -200 to -150 ns and 150 to 200 ns (far outside the range of direct neutronneutron events) and that average rate was subtracted from the doubles rate as a function of detection time diﬀerence. The accidental background rate was less than 0.01% of the doubles rate. Neutrons from the same ﬁssion of roughly the same energy arrive at the detectors at the same time and contribute to the distribution at 0 ns time diﬀerence. Neutrons from the same ﬁssion event, but with diﬀerent energies, would primarily contribute to the distribution away from 0 ns. Also, neutrons scattered from other detectors, ﬂoor, or detector holder primarily contribute away from 0 ns. The cross-talk and room return events appear as shoulders on the narrower, direct-coincidence peak.The 50.4-cm distributions are broader than the 20.4-cm distributions because the increased ﬂight path causes the neutron arrival times to be more widely distributed.

## 4. Conclusions

Previous work has discussed recently added features to DRiFT which produce correlated quantities for organic scintillators and here we show a validation of results from those features. The comparisons in Figs. 5 through 10 indicate that the DRiFT detector response code preserves correlated neutron quantities from MCNP with FREYA ﬁssion events. Some deviations in correlated quantities exist, but those deviations are attributed to limitations in the ﬁssion models used. Validated simulation capabilities are important to develop novel nuclear safeguards and non-proliferation systems as well as to understand existing systems. Future work should include the addition of other common detector types to DRiFT. New types could include gas, inorganic scintillator, and semiconductor detector types. These additions should also be capable of capturing correlated quantities.
